newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. car industry chief favors weaker dollar vs. yen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. car industry chief favors weaker dollar vs. yen.

text.p: The leader of a major U.S. car industry group said Wednesday that the dollar should be around 100 Japanese yen, as a weaker yen hurts U.S. car makers' competitiveness in Japan.

American Automobile Manufacturers Association President Andrew Card said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that the dollar at 110 yen could hurt the progress Tokyo and Washington have made since reaching a bilateral car trade pact last year.
"I think the yen-dollar relationship ... should be more in the neighbourhood of 100 yen per dollar," he said.
The dollar was trading at 109.23 yen in New York at midday on Wednesday. This compares with its record low of 79.75 yen reached in April 1995.
"I think once the yen hits 110 yen per dollar, it puts a tremendous strain on the ability of GM, Ford and Chrysler to meet the expectations of Japanese consumers," he said.
He said he expected sales of American car parts in Japan to drop due to the yen's weakness.

Commenting on a remark by U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor Tuesday that the dollar's recent strength against the yen appeared not to have hurt U.S. car sales in Japan, Card said Kantor may have made "a plain mistake."
Kantor, speaking to reporters in Washington in answer to a question on the dollar's recent strength, had said, "It appears not to have had any adverse effect whatsoever on our ability to sell cars."
A strong dollar against the yen makes U.S. manufacturers less competitive in the Japanese market because it makes their products more expensive in yen terms.
